# FEBRUARY <term>Hornung</term> <gloss>February</gloss>.

<meta>An ornamental decorative initial D begins the first paragraph.</meta>

On February 1st, an <term>Oppositio Saturni Veneris</term> <gloss>opposition of Saturn and Venus</gloss> occurs, stirring up gloomy, frosty air with snow or rain, as also occurred on March 18th, 1513; November 16th, 1562; October 28th, 1589, and others. This significance is increased because around February 2nd, the <term>cauda Capricorni praecedens & sequens</term> <gloss>preceding and following stars in the tail of Capricorn</gloss> rise with the Sun in the morning. This rising commonly causes increasing cold, thick fogs, and subsequent fair weather with frost and sharp winds.

The Full Light <note>the full moon</note>, which falls on the Feast of the Purification of Mary and occurs on February 3rd, will for the most part cause foggy air with unstable sunshine. At that same time, the Sun rises <term>cum Apice Trianguli</term> <gloss>with the peak of the Triangle constellation</gloss>, giving unstable air or snow and sharp winds. Around the 8th, the <term>cauda Delphini</term> <gloss>tail of the Dolphin</gloss> sets with the Sun in the evening; this softens and dissolves the ice and snow, creating great floods of water and gloomy, foggy air with winds. On the 9th, a <term>Quadratus Martis Solis</term> <gloss>square of Mars and the Sun</gloss> takes place, bringing a release from the cold and gloomy weather, as happened on December 28th, 1556; December 4th, 1586; January 5th, 1589; and January 18th and 19th, 1574. On those last two days, such a cold was experienced as had not been seen for some time, but afterward, for several days, rain with soft snow followed, and the cold soon subsided. The last quarter moon occurs on February 10th. This will be moist and very windy. On February 11th, the Sun sets <term>cum Rhomboide delphini Australi</term> <gloss>with the Southern Rhomboid of the Dolphin</gloss>, as it also does on the 12th <term>cum Rhomboide delphini Boreali</term> <gloss>with the Northern Rhomboid of the Dolphin</gloss>; here the weather ends and rain or soft snow follows. On the 13th, a <term>Quadratus Martis Mercurij</term> <gloss>square of Mars and Mercury</gloss> occurs, giving strong winds, dark clouds, and unstable weather, as was experienced on January 23rd, 1591. καὶ θάτερον ἐφαρμόττει· οἷον τῇ γραμμῇ ὑπάρχει καθ’ αὑτὸ τὸ μῆκος· ἐν γὰρ τῷ τί ἐστι κατηγορεῖται, καὶ οὐ μόνον γε καθ’ αὑτὸ ἀλλὰ καὶ ᾗ αὐτό. καὶ τὸ εὐθὺ πάλιν ὑπάρχει τῇ γραμμῇ καθ’ αὑτὸ καὶ ᾗ αὐτό· ὃ γάρ ἐστιν ὁρισμὸς τοῦ εὐθὺ δίχα τῆς γραμμῆς. ἆρ’ οὖν ἅπαντα καθόλου κατηγορεῖται, ὅσα ἐν τῷ ὁρισμῷ τινὸς παραλαμβάνεται; ταῦτα δ’ ἐστὶ τὰ γένη καὶ αἱ διαφοραί· ὑπάρχει γὰρ αὐτοῖς καὶ τὸ καὶ παντὸς εἶναι καὶ τὸ καθ’ αὑτό. ἢ δεῖ καὶ τρίτης προσθήκης εἰς τὸ ἀκριβῶς ὁρίσασθαι τὸ καθόλου; δεῖ γὰρ τὸ καθόλου, πρὸς τῷ παντὶ ὑπάρχειν καὶ καθ’ αὑτὸ ὑπάρχειν, ἔτι καὶ πρώτῳ ἐκείνῳ ὑπάρχειν καὶ οὐδενὶ ἄλλῳ προτέρῳ. <margin>Themist. f. 3 b.</margin>

ἀπαριθμησάμενος τὰ τοῦ καθ’ αὑτὸ σημαινόμενα καὶ ἀφορισάμενος τὰ χρήσιμα πάσης τῆς ἀποδεικτικῆς μεθόδου, μέτεισιν εἰς τὴν περὶ τοῦ καθόλου διδασκαλίαν. τρία δὲ οἶδε τοῦ καθόλου τὰ σημαινόμενα ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης, ἓν μὲν τὸ ἁπλῶς ὑποκειμένῳ παντὶ ὑπάρχειν τὸ κατηγορούμενον, κἂν μὴ καθ’ αὑτὸ ὑπάρχῃ, ὡς φαμὲν παντὶ Αἰθίοπι τὸ μέλαν ἢ παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ βαδίζειν· δεύτερον δὲ ὃ καθόλου τέ ἐστι καὶ καθ’ αὑτό, ὡς φαμὲν πάσῃ δεκάδι τὸ ἄρτιον· τρίτον δὲ ὃ καθ’ αὑτό τέ ἐστι καὶ ᾗ αὐτὸ καὶ πρώτως, ὅπερ νῦν καὶ παραδίδωσι καὶ ταῖς ἀποδεικτικαῖς παραλαμβάνειν μεθόδους, οἷον τὸ παντὶ τριγώνῳ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας εἶναι... τὸ γὰρ τοῦτο φησὶ τὸ καθόλου εἰς τὴν ἀπόδειξιν δεῖν παραλαμβάνειν. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, συμβήσεται μηδὲν εἶναι ἀποδεικτικὸν ἃ μὴ ἀντιστρέφει πρὸς τὸ κατηγορούμενον, χρὴ ἵνα συντόμως εἴπω, μόνας εἶναι τοὺς ὁρισμοὺς καὶ τὰ ἴδια ἀποδεικτικὰ διὰ τὸ ἀντιστρέφειν πρὸς τὰ ὁριστά, τὸ μέντοι ὅτι ὁ ἄνθρωπος ζῷόν ἐστι μὴ εἶναι ἀποδεικτόν, διότι μὴ πρώτως τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ τὸ κατηγορούμενον ὑπάρχει. καὶ φησὶ πρὸς τοῦτο ὁ Θεμίστιος ὅτι εἰ τὰ γένη καὶ αἱ διαφοραὶ τῶν ἀποδεικτικῶν, αἳ οὐ μὴ ἐξισάζουσι πρὸς τὰ ὑποκείμενα, ἀλλ’ οὖν ἐπειδὴ καθ’ αὑτό τε καὶ παντὶ τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ ὑπάρχουσι. καὶ δῆλον ὅτι ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης τὴν κυριωτάτην καὶ μάλιστα ἀπόδειξιν τὴν τῷ πρώτῳ πρέπουσαν φιλοσόφῳ διασκοπούμενος, ταύτην φησὶν εἶναι τὴν καθολικώτατα δεικνύουσαν. δῆλον οὖν ὅτι δευτέρα ἂν εἴη μέτρα ἀποδείξεως τὰ ἐπὶ τῶν γενῶν καὶ τῶν διαφορῶν παραλαμβανόμενα, πρῶτα δὲ ἃ μάλιστα ὅπερ αὐτὸς παρέδωκε. τινὲς δὲ πρὸς τούτῳ κἀκεῖνο ἔφασαν, ὡς ταὐτά φησιν ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης ὅτι ὅτι πάντα τὰ ἀποδεικτικὰ ὀφείλει ἀντιστρέφειν, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα τὰ συμβαλλόμενα πρὸς τὴν ἀπόδειξιν. οἷον ἐν τῇ ἀποδείξει τοῦ τὸ τρίγωνον τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν, παραληπτέον ὅτι ἐὰν εἰς δύο εὐθείας παραλλήλους εὐθεῖα ἐμπέσῃ, τὰς ἐναλλὰξ τρεῖς γωνίας ἴσας ἀλλήλαις ποιεῖ· καὶ ἔστι τοῦτο ἀντιστρέφον· ἐν ᾧ γὰρ αἱ ἐναλλὰξ τρεῖς γωνίαι ἴσαι ἀλλήλαις εἰσίν, ἐκεῖ εἰς δύο παραλλήλους εὐθείας εὐθεῖα ἐμπέπτωκε. τοῦτο δέ ἐσι ψεῦδος· οὐ γὰρ τοῦτό φησιν ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης, ἀλλὰ περὶ αὐτῶν τῶν ἀποδεικτικῶν τὸν λόγον ποιεῖται, ὡς ἐν τῇ λέξει ἐπισημειωσόμεθα... ἰστέον τοίνυν ὅτι ὁ μὲν Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν τούτοις τὸ αὐτὸ φησὶν εἶναι τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ καὶ τὸ ᾗ αὐτό· εἰ τί μὴ ᾗ αὐτό, τοῦτο οὐ καθ’ αὑτό. οἱ δὲ περὶ τὸν Θεόφραστον διαφέρειν ταῦτα λέγουσι· καθολικώτερον γὰρ εἶναι τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ τοῦ ᾗ αὐτό· εἴ τι μὲν ᾗ αὐτό, τοῦτο καὶ καθ’ αὑτό, οὐκ εἴ τι δὲ καθ’ αὑτό, πάντως καὶ ᾗ αὐτό. τῷ γὰρ τριγώνῳ ᾗ τρίγωνόν ἐστιν ὑπάρχει τὸ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθ’ αὑτό· τῷ δὲ ἰσοσκελεῖ καθ’ αὑτὸ μὲν ὑπάρχει, οὐκέτι δὲ ᾗ αὐτό· ᾗ γὰρ ᾗ ἰσοσκελὲς ὑπάρχει αὐτῷ τὸ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν· εἰ γὰρ τοῦτο, οὐκ ἂν τῷ ἰσοπλεύρῳ ἢ σκαληνῷ ὑπῆρχεν, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἰσοσκελῆ, ἀλλ’ ἢ ἁπλῶς τρίγωνά ἐστιν. ταῦτα μὲν οἱ περὶ Θεόφραστον, ὁ μέντοι Ἀριστοτέλης εὑρὼν ἐπί τινων ταῦτα συντρέχοντα ταὐτὸν εἶναι ἔφη ἄμφω· τὸ γὰρ νῦν καὶ ἐπιστήμης δεκτικὸν καθ’ αὑτό τε ὑπάρχει τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ ᾗ αὐτό· εἰ γὰρ ᾗ ζῷόν ἐστι And straightness, again, belongs to a line essentially and as such; for it is the definition of "straight" without the line. Are, then, all things predicated universally, which are taken up in the definition of something? These are the genera and the differences; for both "belonging to every" and "belonging essentially" apply to them. Or is a third addition necessary to define the universal precisely? For the universal must, in addition to belonging to every instance and belonging essentially, also belong to that first subject and to no other prior to it. <margin>Themistius, fol. 3b.</margin>

Having enumerated the meanings of "essentially" and having defined those useful for the entire demonstrative method, he proceeds to the teaching concerning the universal. Aristotle recognizes three meanings of the universal: first, that the predicate belongs to every subject simply, even if it does not belong essentially, as we say "black" belongs to every Ethiopian or "walking" to every human; second, that which is both universal and essential, as we say "even" belongs to every decad; and third, that which is essential, as such, and primarily, which he now hands down and takes up for demonstrative methods, for example, that "the three angles of every triangle are equal to two right angles"... for he says that this is the universal that must be taken up for demonstration. If this is so, it will follow that nothing is demonstrative that does not convert with the predicate; it is necessary, to speak briefly, that only definitions and proper attributes are demonstrative because they convert with the defined, whereas the fact that "a human is an animal" is not demonstrable, because the predicate does not belong to the subject primarily. And Themistius says regarding this that if the genera and differences are demonstrative, which do not equal the subjects, they are so because they belong essentially and to every subject. And it is clear that Aristotle, examining the most authoritative and primary demonstration suitable for a philosopher, says this is the one that demonstrates most universally. It is clear, therefore, that the things taken up regarding genera and differences would be a second measure of demonstration, and those which he himself handed down are the first. Some, in addition to this, said that Aristotle says the same thing, that all demonstrative things ought to convert, but these are the things that contribute to the demonstration. For example, in the demonstration that "a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles," one must take up that "if a straight line falls upon two parallel straight lines, it makes the alternate angles equal to each other"; and this is convertible; for where the alternate angles are equal to each other, there a straight line has fallen upon two parallel straight lines. But this is false; for Aristotle does not say this, but makes his argument about the demonstrative things themselves, as we shall note in the text... One must know, therefore, that Aristotle in these passages says that "essentially" and "as such" are the same; if something is not "as such," it is not "essentially." But those around Theophrastus say these differ; for "essentially" is more universal than "as such"; if something is "as such," it is also "essentially," but if something is "essentially," it is not necessarily "as such." For to a triangle, as it is a triangle, it belongs to have three angles equal to two right angles, but it also belongs essentially; but to an isosceles triangle it belongs essentially, but no longer as such; for it does not belong to it as it is isosceles to have three angles equal to two right angles; for if this were so, it would not belong to the equilateral or scalene, since they are not isosceles, but are simply triangles. These are the views of those around Theophrastus, but Aristotle, having found these coinciding in some cases, said both were the same; for the capacity for knowledge belongs to a human both essentially and as such; for if it is as a living being that it is capable of knowledge, then not even a horse or any ensouled being, but only a human; for this alone of living beings seems to be capable of knowledge. And to an odd number, the inability to be divided into equal parts belongs essentially and as such. <margin>John Philoponus, fol. 17.</margin>

This, therefore, is the third determination of the universal. And "in any given case" <margin>32.</margin> means when the predicate belongs to any given instance of the subject, for example, to any given triangle it belongs to have three angles equal to two right angles, and not only to the given instance but also primarily; for it belongs to the triangle primarily, even if it belongs to the scalene, that it has three angles equal to two right angles. <margin>id., fol. 17b.</margin>

He observes how clearly he says through these that the things useful for demonstration are, as I was saying, the demonstrative ones; for he says that demonstration itself is also essential and universal. <margin>id., ibid.</margin> <margin>40.</margin>

One must not fail to notice that we are often deceived concerning the universal <margin>74a 4.</margin> and, not demonstrating it as we think we are demonstrating, we think we are demonstrating when we are not. There are three causes of this deception: one is when we make demonstrations about some particular or individual thing, for example, the sun, the moon, the cosmos; since there is nothing above these nor anything common, but the individual is in each case (for there is one sun, one moon, one earth, and one heaven), when we demonstrate something belonging to these, such as the earth lying in the center or the heaven moving in a circle, we do not think we are demonstrating it as belonging universally, even though we do not make the demonstration according to what each of these is as an individual. For if we demonstrate that the sun is eclipsed when the moon runs under it, such are the demonstrations that occur as if there were more, it would fit them likewise. <margin>Themistius, fol. 3b.</margin>

Having taught concerning the universal, he now wishes to hand down the causes of the deception, according to which we often think we are demonstrating universally when we are not demonstrating what the universal is and what is handed down here. He says there are three causes of such deception: one is when there is something unique and individual, about which we make demonstrations, for example, that the earth lies in the center of the whole, or that the cosmos is spherical, or the symptoms that happen specifically to the sun... these would not be universal, because it is not because there is one earth nor because there is one sun that these things happen to them, but because it is simply "sun" and because it is simply "earth," so that if there were more, these would fit them as well. Therefore, the things demonstrated in those cases are not demonstrated universally. <margin>John Philoponus, fol. 17b.</margin>

The Emperor was at Trento when he made this concession, and he made it known that he wanted to pass into Italy, from which many wars followed in Lombardy, through which the Viscontis took possession of Parma. At this time, Robert, King of Naples, died, and there remained only two granddaughters born of his son Charles, who had died some time before. He restored it to its ancient form with such a reputation for justice and virtue that not only the nearby lands, but all of Italy sent him ambassadors, such that the ancient provinces, seeing how Rome was reborn, lifted their heads, and some moved by fear, some by hope, honored him. But Niccolò, despite such a reputation, abandoned himself in his beginnings; because, invited under such a weight, without being driven out by anyone,<note>original: "Aggiungi che fu osteggiato dai nobili e abbandonato dal popolo, cui era divenuto increscioso, dicesi per il suo vano sfarzo, e perchè il buono stato da lui predicato non corrispose poi alle aspettazioni al solito esorbitanti." <gloss>Add that he was opposed by the nobles and abandoned by the people, to whom he had become tiresome, it is said because of his vain ostentation, and because the good state he preached did not then correspond to the usually exorbitant expectations.</gloss></note> he secretly fled and went to find Charles, King of Bohemia, who by order of the Pope, in contempt of Louis of Bavaria, had been elected Emperor.<note>original: "Carlo IV." <gloss>Charles IV.</gloss></note> This man, to gratify the Pontiff, sent him Niccolò as a prisoner.

μίτιδος non autem παρθενίου. Neque inde tamen nobis facile persuadebitur hanc non esse veram genuinamque Clementis nostri vocem. Nulli siquidem dubitamus ab illo sensum potius Platonis quam verba exhiberi. Quapropter si nullus ibi ipsius memoriæ lapsus fuerit, vocem παρθενίου potius quam κεραμίτιδος ab eo usurpatam credimus, tum quia utraque vox idem significat, quando quidem creta est terra, qua nemo unquam usus fuit; tum quia ea vox ad suum de sacra Scriptura, quam ille, ut infra dicetur, cum Virgine Deipara alibi componit, propositum magis faciebat. Has porro voces παρθενίου γῆς, quas Hervetus nullibi se legisse dicit, ab alio in suis ad Clementis nostri opera scholiis scite observatur in Nicandri *Alexipharmacis* reperiri. Addamus obiter, si velis, alio sensu virginem terram a Tertulliano accipi pro terra nec pluviis rigata, nec imbribus fecundata, ex qua Adam et Christus plasmati sunt: « Utique, inquit, illa terra virgo, nondum pluviis rigata, nec imbribus fecundata, ex qua homo tunc primum plasmatus est, ex qua nunc Christus secundum carnem ex virgine natus est ¹⁶. »

*Stromatum* suorum argumenta ubi paulo post Clemens explicat, ex illis unum sic proponit: Καὶ τούτοις ἀντερεῖ πάνθ' ὅσα προοικονομηθῆναι καθήκει τῆς κατὰ **140** τὴν ὑποπτικὴν θεωρίαν γνώσεως ¹⁷. Quod in ultima editione sic Latine redditum est: « Et adversus ea dicet, quæcunque ante propheticam contemplationem prius dispensata esse oportet. » Atque ita quidem Hervetus se prius ex Clementis Græcis Latina olim fecisse aperte declarat. Sed re maturius expensa, pro ὑποπτικὴν legendum esse ait ἐποπτικὴν θεωρίαν, hoc est « inspectivam seu speculatoriam contemplationem. » Vult enim Clementem ibi alludere ad mysteria Græcorum, quibus ea cum aspicere liceret, tunc, ut infra dicemus ¹⁸, hi ἐπόπται vocabantur. Qui tamen posteriori horum *Stromatum* editioni præfuerunt, spreta illa Herveti correctione, quæ sensui auctoris omnino consentanea ipsis forsitan non videbatur, verbum Græcum ὑποπτικὴν, et Latinum « propheticam » censuerunt esse retinendum. Et vero in Græco nostro manuscripto codice idem verbum habetur. Nihil ergo in textu Græco, nisi accedat major alterius cujusdam manuscripti auctoritas, quidquam mutandum est. Vox autem ὑποπτικὴ quid ibi significet si roges, tibi respondebimus ὕποπτος, teste Julio Polluce, non solum idem ac « suspectus, » sed quandoque « inspiciens, » significare. Quamobrem illius interpres verbum ὕποπτοι Latine « inspectores » reddidit. Atqui vox ὑποπτικὴ si eo significatu accipi possit, hic Clementis locus in Latinum sermonem ita convertendus est: « Atque (sermo noster) ea indicabit quæcunque aut dispensari convenit ante inspicientis seu inspectricis contemplationis cognitionem, γνώσεως. » Verbum enim ἀντέρω interdum « renuntio, denuntio et indico » significare certum est. Eo porro significatu illud, atque ipso, quo diximus, sensu vocem ὑποπτικὴν ibi a Clemente usurpari ex his, quæ continuo ille subtexuit, et ipsismet, quæ in toto opere pertractat, argumentis haud obscure colligitur. Si quis vero aliam veriorem horum verborum interpretationem, aliumque sincerum illorum sensum assecutus fuerit, hunc nobis si suggerere voluerit, maximas sane et debitas ei gratias referemus.

Notat porro Hervetus alibi Clementis textui tenebras perquam densissimas offundi, atque in illo librariorum oscitantia aliquid depravatum vel hiulcum et mutilum esse, ubi Mosaicæ legis benignitate eo demonstrata argumento, quia arbores nuper plantatas tribus annis ali et foveri, quartoque anno eas Deo consecrari jubet, hæc Clemens subjunxit:

<column-break/>

« Quarto anno, quoniam tempore quoque opus est ei, qui stabiliter per catechesin instituitur, quaternio virtutum Deo consecratur, cum tertia jam sola subjungatur cum quarta Domini hypostasi; sacrificium autem laudis super holocausta. » Τῷ τε γὰρ τετάρτῳ ἔτει, ἐπεὶ καὶ χρόνου χρεία τῷ κατηχουμένῳ βεβαίως, ἡ τετρὰς τῶν ἀρετῶν καθιεροῦται τῷ Θεῷ τῆς τρίτης ἤδη μόνης συναπτούσης ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου τετάρτην ὑπόστασιν. Θυσία δὲ αἰνέσεως ὑπὲρ ὁλοκαυτώματα ¹⁹. Hervetus itaque hæc se non intelligere fatetur. Conjicit tamen, « ex hoc intelligi, » ita ille loquitur, « perfectam illam esse fidem, quæ tres complectitur hypostases, seu personas, quarum tertia, nempe Filii hypostasis, sola conjungitur cum quarta hypostasi Domini, nempe cum humana natura. » Quæ quidem cum ante susceptam a Filio carnem, ab ejus persona esset separata, videtur aliqua ratione dici posse quarta hypostasis, tametsi reapse in Christo, humana carne induto, una tantum divina persona sit. Quocirca nos serio ea de re monitos esse vult, ne inde in Nestorii errorem imprudentes prolabamur.

Sed tantum abest ut hac explicatione obscura hujus loci discutiatur caligo; quin ei potius longe major aspergatur. Quis enim facile sibi persuadeat Clementem ibi de triplici Dei persona, et de quarta improprie dicta humanitatis Christi hypostasi fuisse locutum? Quomodo in illum de divinis personis, de quibus nihil plane neque prius, neque posterius dicit vel insinuat, sermonem delapsus est? Qua denique ratione Hervetus probabit ibi Clementem verbo ὑπόστασις personam, seu, ut aiunt, personalitatem intellexisse. Neminem certe fugit ab antiquis scriptoribus, qui ante et post Clementis ætatem scripserunt, illud nomen ad naturam, seu idem atque οὐσία, significandum sæpissime adhiberi. Quin etiam si Hieronymo credamus: « Tota sæcularium litterarum schola nihil aliud hypostasin, nisi usiam novit ²⁰. »

Nobis ergo Clementem non de divinis personis, sed de quaternione virtutum, quas vulgo cardinales nuncupant, loqui facilius probabitur. Vox enim ὑπόστασις ibi nihil aliud significare videtur, quam id quod stat et subsistit, seu firmum rei alicujus semperque immobilem consistendi statum. Quamobrem verum Clementis sensum hunc esse putamus: quaternio virtutum Deo consecratur, tertia sola, nimirum justitia, hominem quartæ Domini ὑποστάσει, hoc est firmo nec mutationis amplius obnoxio Domini statui conjungente. Vult enim doctus ille vir, hac quaternione virtutum hominem Christianum Deo, quoad ejus fieri potest, assimilari, ac quiescentibus animi perturbationibus, ad permanentem nullique mutationi obnoxium Dei statum, quantum fieri licet, accedere, pervenire ac ipsi inhærere. Hanc porro esse Clementis mentem ea plane demonstrant, quæ ille dixerat de quatuor illis virtutibus, atque ibidem de « gnostico, » seu perfecto Christiano addidit: « Hic est enim, inquit, ad Dei imaginem et similitudinem gnosticus, qui Deum imitatur, quoad ejus fieri potest, nihil prætermittens eorum, quæ faciunt ad eam, quæ contingere potest, similitudinem, continens, sustinens, juste vivens, imperans animi perturbationibus, ea quæ habet impartiens, pro viribus benefaciens et verbo et opere. » Subsequentia porro verba: « Sacrificium laudis super holocausta, » quomodo cum superioribus cohæreant, etiamsi dictu difficillimum esse fateamur, eorum tamen is sensus dici potest: Hanc virtutum quaternionem qui adeptus fuerit, ab illo sacrificium, holocautomatis longe præstantius, ipsimet Deo offerri. Si quis nihilominus aliam ostendat fuisse auctoris nostri mentem, huic manus dabimus, atque nos ab eo vinci lubenter patiemur.

of potter's clay <note>original: "κεραμίτιδος"</note>, not "virgin" <note>original: "παρθενίου"</note>. Yet this will not easily persuade us that the latter is not the true and genuine word of our Clement. For we have no doubt at all that he is giving the sense of Plato rather than his exact words. Therefore, unless his memory slipped at this point, we believe that he used the word "virgin" rather than "of potter's clay." First, because both words mean the same thing, since chalk is earth that no one has ever used. Second, because that word better served his purpose with regard to Sacred Scripture, which, as will be said below, he elsewhere compares with the Virgin Mother of God <note>original: "Virgine Deipara"</note>. Moreover, these words "virgin earth" <note>original: "παρθενίου γῆς"</note>, which Hervetus says he never read anywhere, are shrewdly observed by another scholar, in his notes on the works of our Clement, to be found in the *Alexipharmaca* of Nicander. <note>Gentian Hervet (Hervetus) was a sixteenth-century French humanist who translated Clement into Latin. Nicander of Colophon wrote the Alexipharmaca, a Greek poem on poisons and their antidotes.</note> Let us add in passing, if you like, that Tertullian takes "virgin earth" in another sense: earth not yet watered by rains nor made fruitful by showers, from which Adam and Christ were formed. "Certainly," he says, "that earth was a virgin, not yet watered by rains nor made fertile by showers, from which man was then first formed, just as now Christ according to the flesh was born of a virgin ¹⁶."

Where Clement, a little later, sets out the subjects of his *Stromata*, he proposes one of them as follows: "And it will speak in reply to all those things which ought to be arranged beforehand for the knowledge that belongs to the **140** 'hypoptic' contemplation ¹⁷." <note>original: "Καὶ τούτοις ἀντερεῖ πάνθ' ὅσα προοικονομηθῆναι καθήκει τῆς κατὰ τὴν ὑποπτικὴν θεωρίαν γνώσεως"</note> In the most recent edition this was rendered into Latin thus: "And it will speak against those things which must first be arranged before prophetic contemplation." Hervetus openly declares that he had once made this Latin version from Clement's Greek. But after weighing the matter more maturely, he says that instead of *hypoptikēn* one should read *epoptikēn theōrian*, that is, "inspective or speculative contemplation." He holds that Clement is alluding here to the mysteries of the Greeks: those who were permitted to behold them were then called *epoptai* <gloss>beholders, the highest grade of initiates</gloss>, as we shall explain below ¹⁸. Those who oversaw the later edition of these *Stromata*, however, rejected Hervetus's correction, which perhaps did not seem to them fully consistent with the author's meaning. They judged that the Greek word *hypoptikēn* and the Latin "prophetic" should be kept. And indeed the same word is found in our Greek manuscript. Nothing in the Greek text should therefore be changed, unless the greater authority of some other manuscript is brought forward.

If you ask what the word *hypoptikē* means here, we will answer that *hypoptos*, according to Julius Pollux, means not only "suspected" but sometimes also "one who inspects." <note>Julius Pollux was a second-century Greek grammarian whose Onomasticon is a thesaurus of Greek vocabulary.</note> For this reason his translator rendered the word *hypoptoi* in Latin as "inspectors." Now, if *hypoptikē* can be taken in that sense, this passage of Clement should be turned into Latin as follows: "And (our discourse) will set forth all those things that ought to be arranged before the knowledge <note>original: "γνώσεως"</note> of inspecting, or observing, contemplation." For it is certain that the verb *anterō* sometimes means "I announce, declare, and indicate." That Clement uses the verb in this meaning, and the word *hypoptikē* in the sense we have given, can be gathered quite clearly from what he immediately adds, and from the very subjects he treats throughout the whole work. But if anyone arrives at another, truer interpretation of these words and their genuine sense, and is willing to suggest it to us, we shall give that person the greatest and most deserved thanks.

Hervetus further notes that elsewhere very thick darkness is cast over Clement's text, and that through the carelessness of copyists something in it has been corrupted, left gaping, or mutilated. This is the passage where Clement shows the kindness of the Mosaic Law by the argument that it commands newly planted trees to be nourished and tended for three years, and in the fourth year consecrated to God. <note>See Leviticus 19:23–25.</note> To this Clement added the following:

<column-break/>

"In the fourth year, since time is also needed by one who is being firmly instructed through catechesis, the foursome of the virtues is consecrated to God, the third alone now joining with the fourth hypostasis of the Lord; and the sacrifice of praise is above burnt offerings." <note>original: "Τῷ τε γὰρ τετάρτῳ ἔτει, ἐπεὶ καὶ χρόνου χρεία τῷ κατηχουμένῳ βεβαίως, ἡ τετρὰς τῶν ἀρετῶν καθιεροῦται τῷ Θεῷ τῆς τρίτης ἤδη μόνης συναπτούσης ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου τετάρτην ὑπόστασιν. Θυσία δὲ αἰνέσεως ὑπὲρ ὁλοκαυτώματα"</note> ¹⁹ Hervetus admits that he does not understand this. Still, he conjectures, in his own words, "that from this we are to understand that faith is perfect which embraces three hypostases, or persons, of which the third, namely the hypostasis of the Son, alone is joined with the fourth hypostasis of the Lord, namely with the human nature." Since the human nature was separate from the Son's person before he took on flesh, it seems that in some way it could be called a fourth hypostasis, even though in reality there is only one divine person in Christ, clothed in human flesh. For this reason Hervetus wants us to be seriously warned not to slip unawares into the error of Nestorius. <note>Nestorius, fifth-century bishop of Constantinople, was condemned for teaching what opponents saw as a division of Christ into two persons.</note>

But this explanation is so far from dispelling the darkness of the passage that it rather spreads a much greater darkness over it. Who could easily persuade himself that Clement was speaking here about the three persons of God, and about a "fourth hypostasis," improperly so called, of Christ's humanity? How would he have slipped into a discussion of the divine persons, about which he says or hints nothing at all either before or after? And finally, how will Hervetus prove that Clement here understood by the word *hypostasis* a person, or, as they say, personality? Surely no one is unaware that ancient writers, both before and after Clement's time, very often used that word to mean nature, that is, the same as *ousia* <gloss>essence, substance</gloss>. Indeed, if we believe Jerome: "The whole school of secular learning knows *hypostasis* as nothing other than *ousia* ²⁰."

It will therefore be easier for us to prove that Clement is speaking not of the divine persons but of the foursome of virtues commonly called cardinal. <note>The four cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.</note> The word *hypostasis* here seems to mean nothing other than that which stands and subsists, that is, the firm and ever-immovable state of a thing's existence. We therefore think Clement's true meaning is this: the foursome of the virtues is consecrated to God, while the third alone, namely justice, joins the human being to the fourth *hypostasis* of the Lord, that is, to the firm state of the Lord that is no longer subject to change. For that learned man means that through this foursome of virtues the Christian is made like God, as far as possible, and that, once the passions of the soul are at rest, he approaches, reaches, and clings to the permanent and unchanging state of God, so far as is allowed.

That this is Clement's thought is plainly shown by what he had said about those four virtues, and by what he added in the same place about the "gnostic," that is, the perfect Christian: "For this," he says, "is the gnostic made after the image and likeness of God, who imitates God as far as he can, neglecting nothing that leads to the likeness that is attainable: self-controlled, enduring, living justly, ruling over the passions of the soul, sharing what he has, doing good as far as he is able, both in word and in deed." As for the following words, "the sacrifice of praise is above burnt offerings," we admit it is very hard to say how they connect with what precedes. Yet their sense can be stated thus: whoever has attained this foursome of virtues offers to God himself a sacrifice far more excellent than a burnt offering. If anyone nevertheless shows that our author meant something else, we shall yield to that person and gladly let ourselves be overcome.

The present **Stereometric lines** <note>A specialized scale on the instrument where divisions are proportional to the cube roots of numbers, used for calculating volumes and scaling three-dimensional objects</note> are so named because their division is according to the proportion of solid bodies, up to 148. From these we will derive many uses, the first of which shall be the one already proposed: namely, how—given one side of any solid body—one can find the side of another which has a given proportion to it. 

For example, let line **A** be the diameter, for instance <note>original: "v.g.", an abbreviation for the Latin *verbi gratia*</note>, of a sphere—or a "ball," to use more common speech—or perhaps the side of a cube or other solid. Let it be proposed to us that we must find the diameter or side of another [solid] that has the same proportion to the first as 20 has to 36. Take line **A** with the compasses <note>referring to a pair of dividers used to transfer distances</note> and, opening the instrument, apply this measurement transversally to point 36 of the **Stereometric lines**.
